title: Inventory Service API
summary: Fix a PATCH endpoint that quietly resets product data, add stock transfers and a paginated product search, then keep the low-stock report fast on a 20,000-product catalogue and make transfers safe to retry.
overview:
You've joined the team behind **Stockroom**, the inventory API that powers the warehouse dashboard for a small chain of tea and coffee shops. It tracks the product catalogue, the warehouses that hold stock, and every movement of stock in or out. Buyers rely on its low-stock report to decide what to reorder.

The service is a FastAPI app with a conventional layered layout: thin routers in `app/routers/`, business rules in `app/services/inventory.py`, an in-memory repository standing in for the database in `app/repository.py`, Pydantic v2 models in `app/schemas.py`, and one error format for every failure in `app/errors.py`.

Start with `README.md` (it documents every endpoint, status code and the error format), then `app/main.py` and the service. `demo.py` seeds a small catalogue and prints a few requests and responses. Tests use FastAPI's `TestClient`, so nothing listens on a port.

phases.title: Edits that undo themselves
phases.instructions:
Two reports came in from the buying team this week:

> *"I changed the price of the gooseneck kettle and nothing else. Now it never shows up on the low-stock report, even though we only have three left. Its reorder level reads 0."*

> *"We discontinued an old teapot, then fixed a typo in its name. It's back in the active catalogue and on the reorder list."*

A third, smaller one: sending `{"description": null}` to clear a product's description returns 200 but the old description is still there.

`PATCH /products/{sku}` is documented as a partial update: only the fields in the request body change, and `description` may be cleared with `null`. Find out why it doesn't behave that way and fix it. Validation must keep working: a negative price or a `null` name is still a `422` with code `validation_error`.

**Done when:** all tests in `tests/test_phase1.py` pass.
hints: Reproduce it with the test client: create a product with a reorder level of 8, PATCH only its price, and GET it again. Which fields changed that you didn't send?
Look at how `ProductUpdate` is defined in `app/schemas.py`. Which fields does it inherit, and what defaults come with them? Then look at how `update_product` turns the request into changes.
Pydantic knows which fields were actually present in the request (`model_fields_set`). `exclude_none` drops `null` values, which is the wrong question: you want to drop fields that were never sent.
phases.answer:
**Root cause.** `ProductUpdate` subclasses `ProductBase`, so it inherits `reorder_level = 0` and `active = True` as defaults. `InventoryService.update_product` applies `changes.model_dump(exclude_none=True)`, which keeps every non-`None` value, including those defaults for fields the client never sent. A price-only PATCH therefore writes `reorder_level = 0` and `active = True`. And because `exclude_none` drops `None`, an explicit `"description": null` is thrown away.

**Fix.** Apply only the fields that were sent:

```python
updated = product.model_copy(update=changes.model_dump(exclude_unset=True))
```

`exclude_unset` uses the set of fields present in the request, so defaults never leak in and an explicit `null` for `description` gets through. The existing model validator still rejects `null` for `name`, `category` and `price_cents`.

**Verify.** PATCH one field and compare the whole product before and after; the phase 1 tests do this for price, name and description.

phases.title: Transfers and product search
phases.instructions:
The dashboard team needs two endpoints. `InventoryService.transfer` and `InventoryService.search_products` are stubs; add the schemas, the service logic and the routes, and register any new router in `create_app`.

### `POST /transfers`

Moves stock of one product between two warehouses. Body: `{"sku", "from_warehouse", "to_warehouse", "quantity", "note"?}`.

- `201` with `{"id": "TR-000001", "sku", "from_warehouse", "to_warehouse", "quantity", "from_on_hand", "to_on_hand"}` (the levels in each warehouse after the move).
- Writes two movements that reference the transfer id: a `transfer_out` from the source, then a `transfer_in` to the destination. The product's total stock does not change.
- `422 validation_error` if `quantity` is not a positive integer (`fields` has `body.quantity`).
- `404 not_found` for an unknown product or warehouse; `400 same_warehouse` if both warehouses are the same.
- `409 insufficient_stock` with `details: {"available", "requested"}` if the source holds too little. A rejected transfer changes nothing.

### `GET /products/search`

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | case-insensitive substring of the name or the SKU |
| `category` | exact category |
| `min_price`, `max_price` | inclusive bounds in cents, each `>= 0`; `min_price > max_price` is `400 invalid_range` |
| `in_stock` | `true`: total stock above 0; `false`: none in any warehouse |
| `sort` | `name` (default, case-insensitive), `price`, `stock`, or the same with a leading `-` for descending; ties always by SKU ascending |
| `page`, `page_size` | 1-based page (`>= 1`), page size 1–100 (default 20) |

Response: `{"items": [{"sku", "name", "category", "price_cents", "on_hand"}], "page", "page_size", "total"}` where `total` counts all matches. A page past the end has no items. Invalid parameters are `422 validation_error` with `fields` such as `query.sort` or `query.page_size`. `GET /products/{sku}` must keep working.

**Done when:** all tests in `tests/test_phase1.py` and `tests/test_phase2.py` pass.
hints: Work layer by layer: request and response models in `schemas.py`, the rules in the service, then a thin route. FastAPI's `Query(ge=..., le=...)` and a `Literal[...]` type for `sort` give you the 422s for free through the existing handler.
If `GET /products/search` returns `404 Product 'search' does not exist`, look at route order: routes are matched in the order they are declared, and `/products/{sku}` matches anything.
For a transfer, check everything (product, both warehouses, same warehouse, available quantity) before changing any stock, then reuse `_apply` for both sides with the transfer id as the reference.
For stable tie-breaking, start from the SKU-ordered list and use a single stable `sort` with `reverse=True` for descending keys: Python keeps equal elements in their original order either way.
phases.answer:
**Transfers.** `TransferRequest` (with `quantity: int = Field(gt=0)`) and `TransferResult` in `schemas.py`; a `transfers.py` router with `POST /transfers` returning 201; `InventoryService.transfer` validates the product and both warehouses (404), rejects the same warehouse (400 `same_warehouse`), checks the source level (409 `insufficient_stock` with `available`/`requested`), takes an id from `repo.next_id("TR")` and calls `_apply` twice (`transfer_out` with a negative delta, then `transfer_in`), both referencing the id.

**Search.** A `/products/search` route declared *before* `/products/{sku}`, with typed `Query` parameters (`sort: Literal[...]`, `page: int = Query(1, ge=1)`, `page_size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100)`, `min_price`/`max_price` with `ge=0`). The service checks the price range (400 `invalid_range`), filters the SKU-ordered product list, computes each product's total stock, sorts with one stable sort (`reverse=True` for a `-` prefix, so ties stay by SKU) and slices the page.

**Complexity.** Search is O(P·W + M log M) for P products, W warehouses and M matches, which is fine for the dashboard's page sizes. Each transfer is O(1).

phases.title: A dashboard that polls, and clients that retry
phases.instructions:
Stockroom is going live for the whole chain: about **20,000 products** across six warehouses.

1. **The low-stock report is too slow.** Every open dashboard tab polls `GET /reports/low-stock` every few seconds while stock moves all day. Today each call walks the whole catalogue and adds up every warehouse for every product. Make the report fast without changing its output: active products whose total stock is below their reorder level, largest shortfall first, then SKU; `total` counts all of them, `items` the first `limit`; the optional `category` filter still works. It must stay correct after movements, transfers, new products, reorder-level changes and products being discontinued.

2. **Retried transfers move stock twice.** The handheld scanners retry a request when the network drops, so one transfer sometimes happens twice. Support an `Idempotency-Key` request header on `POST /transfers`:
   - the same key with the same body returns the original `201` response (same transfer id) and moves nothing;
   - the same key with a different body is `409` with code `idempotency_conflict`;
   - requests without the header behave as before; only successful transfers are remembered.

The tests seed the catalogue by calling the service directly (`app.state.inventory`), so keep `create_product`, `create_warehouse`, `record_movement` and `low_stock_report(category=None, limit=50)` working with the same signatures.

**Done when:** all three test files pass. The timed test runs 200 report refreshes while stock moves and must finish in under 0.6 seconds.
hints: Two costs add up: `on_hand(sku)` loops over every warehouse, and the report loops over every product. Which of those can be kept up to date as stock changes, instead of recomputed on every request?

Keep a running total per SKU in the repository, updated inside `set_quantity`. Then keep the *set* of low-stock SKUs in the service, refreshed for one SKU whenever its stock, reorder level or active flag changes. Only a few hundred products are ever low.
Every path that changes stock goes through `_apply`, and every product change goes through `create_product` or `update_product`: those are the only places that need to refresh the low-stock set.

For idempotency, store `key -> (request body, result)` in the service. Compare the stored body with the new one before deciding between returning the stored result and a 409. Read the header with `Header(default=None)` on a parameter named `idempotency_key`.
phases.answer:
**Maintained aggregates.** The repository keeps `totals[sku]`, updated in `set_quantity` by the difference between the new and old quantity, so `on_hand` is O(1). The service keeps `_low`, the set of active SKUs with `on_hand < reorder_level`, refreshed for one SKU by `_refresh_low` at the end of `_apply`, `create_product` and `update_product`. The report sorts only the low set: O(L log L) for L low-stock products instead of O(P·W) per call. The straightforward version takes several seconds for 200 refreshes at 20,000 products; the aggregate version takes a few tens of milliseconds. A running total alone is not enough: it still visits every product per call.

**Idempotency.** `transfer(data, idempotency_key=None)`: under a lock (sync routes run in a thread pool, so two retries can arrive together), look up the key; if it exists with the same `model_dump()` of the body, return the stored `TransferResult`; with a different body raise `409 idempotency_conflict`; otherwise perform the transfer and store `(body, result)`. Failed transfers are not stored, so a client can fix the problem and retry with the same key. In production the key store would live in the database with an expiry, written in the same transaction as the stock change.

debrief: How did you confirm that the PATCH problem came from defaults leaking in rather than from the repository or the response model, and why is `exclude_unset` the right tool where `exclude_none` was not?
Walk through how a transfer stays all-or-nothing in your implementation. What would you change if two transfers from the same warehouse could run at the same time on a real database?

Which events can move a product into or out of the low-stock set, and how did you check that your maintained aggregate never drifts from a full recomputation? How long would you keep idempotency keys, and where would you store them in production?
